summary: Describes a URN namespace identifier for the International Organization for Standardization, for naming persistent resources it publishes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives the world standards organization its own permanent naming scheme for its documents and data.

questions: how to cite iso standards with urns
subtitle: A persistent naming scheme for ISO standards and technical specifications.

tldr.problem: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) publishes thousands of technical standards and specifications, and they need a persistent, location-independent way to identify and reference these resources.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace identifier called 'iso' that allows ISO to assign unique, permanent identifiers to its standards documents, metadata, and extracted resources. The URN syntax specifies how to encode the document number, type, part number, edition, and other attributes.
tldr.outcome: ISO standards and related resources can now be identified with permanent URNs like urn:iso:std:iso:9999:-1:ed-1:en, enabling reliable citations and references across the internet and within systems.

today: RFC 5141 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. The ISO Central Secretariat continues to use this URN namespace to identify its standards and technical resources.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) is a network of national standards institutes from many countries, with a central secretariat in Geneva. ISO's core mission is to develop technical standards that enable compatible technology worldwide. ISO publishes International Standards, Technical Reports, Guides, and other technical specifications that dictate required or expected practices in many industries across the globe.

These specifications contain dictionaries of standard terms, formal schemata for information exchange, definitions of formal languages, and reference value catalogues. Many are cited in laws, regulations, and industry best practices. The problem: ISO needs globally unique, persistent, location-independent identifiers for these resources that can survive format changes, server migrations, and decades of use.
sections.plainLanguage: ISO makes standards that the whole world uses. They want to give each one a permanent name that never breaks, even if their website moves or standards are updated.

sections.title: The Namespace Syntax
sections.content:
The RFC defines the syntax for URNs that identify ISO documents. All URNs in the 'iso' namespace begin with the prefix urn:iso, followed by a Namespace Specific String (NSS) that encodes the document identity. The NSS structure uses the prefix std: to denote standards developed under ISO's formal procedures, followed by fields separated by colons:

originator:type:docnumber:partnumber:status:edition:docversion:language:supplement:docelement:addition

The originator indicates the standards body (iso, iec, iso-iec, iso-ieee, etc.). The optional type field specifies the deliverable category: tr (Technical Report), ts (Technical Specification), pas (Publicly Available Specification), or others. If omitted, the resource is an International Standard. The docnumber is the reference number assigned by ISO (e.g., 9999 for ISO 9999). The partnumber distinguishes parts of multipart standards. The status indicates publication state (draft, cancelled, or the stage code). The edition, docversion, and language pinpoint a specific edition, version, and language variant.

Additional elements allow URNs to reference extracts from a standard, such as a specific clause, figure, table, or term defined within it, without requiring a separate URN for each part.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN is like a permanent library address. This RFC explains how to write one: you list the organization, the type of document, its number, which part and edition you mean, and which language. Simple parts are optional, so short URNs work too.

sections.title: Examples of ISO URNs
sections.content:
The RFC provides many examples to illustrate the syntax. A basic URN naming ISO standard 9999 part 1 in English, 1st edition is urn:iso:std:iso:9999:-1:ed-1:en. The hyphen before the 1 is a literal part separator. A bilingual version uses urn:iso:std:iso:9999:-1:ed-1:en,fr. A Technical Report (TR) is named like urn:iso:std:iso-iec:tr:9999:-1:ed-1:en. A cancelled or draft document includes the status: urn:iso:std:iso-iec:9075:-3:cancelled:ed-2:en or urn:iso:std:iso-iec:9075:-3:draft:ed-4:en. Draft documents can also use the stage code system, for example urn:iso:std:iso-iec:9075:-3:stage-30.60:ed-4:en, where the code indicates the stage of development. References to all parts of a multipart standard omit the partnumber: urn:iso:std:iso:128:en refers to all parts of ISO 128 in English.

URNs can also reference subdivisions within a document using the :clause:, :figure:, :table:, or :term: element to point to a specific clause number, figure, table or defined term.
sections.plainLanguage: Examples show how the naming works in practice. A single standard is urn:iso:std:iso:9999:-1:ed-1:en. Add a type like :tr: for a Technical Report. Mark status like :draft: or :cancelled:. You can even point to one clause inside a standard.

sections.title: Resolution and Uniqueness
sections.content:
The RFC specifies rules for identifier uniqueness and persistence. Every URN assigned by ISO will conform to the Namespace Specific String (NSS) syntax defined in RFC 2141. The namespace registrant (the ISO Central Secretariat) is responsible for guaranteeing that each assigned NSS is unique and persists indefinitely, even as ISO standards are revised, withdrawn, or succeeded by newer editions.

The RFC also defines lexical equivalence rules: language codes are case-insensitive (so en and EN are equivalent), but this distinction carries no semantic meaning. The resolution process—how a URN is looked up to find the actual document—is left to future specifications; the RFC focuses on the persistent naming scheme itself, not the lookup mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Each URN is unique, so no two standards get the same one. Once ISO assigns a URN, it stays the same forever, even if the standard is updated or withdrawn. Uppercase and lowercase are treated the same way.

sections.title: Scope and Future Extensions
sections.content:
The current specification covers documents developed by ISO under its formal procedures—International Standards, Technical Reports, Technical Specifications, and similar deliverables. It does not extend to products or handbooks derived from ISO standards, nor to documents at or below the Technical Committee level. Future revisions may define syntax for URNs identifying other ISO objects if the ISO community defines requirements for such identifiers.

The RFC also reserves the :tech prefix for resources defined by technical committees (like extracted schemata or value sets), and leaves space for the ISO Central Secretariat to define additional resource types. This forward-looking design allows the URN namespace to grow with ISO's needs without breaking existing URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: This scheme covers ISO's main standards and technical documents, but not related products or items below the committee level. The design leaves room to add new types of resources later if needed.
